title: Flight and plight

The doctrine that flight is evidence of guilt -- but only when unexplained and unrebutted
CJ's call for the SC to decide the GMA travel case via oral argument rather than ex parte TRO

stances.claim: The three flight cases (Ramona, Lacson, GMA) share a common legal thread — the right to travel of suspects in capital, non-bailable offenses — but each is factually unique and must be decided on its specific context, consistent with Holmes's principle that 'general propositions do not decide specific cases.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Holmes-principle application: contextual-uniqueness doctrine as the analytical framework for all three parallel cases

stances.claim: The CA erred by dismissing Lacson's charges while he was still at large — 'encouraging lawlessness and disrespect for the rule of law' — regardless of what the Supreme Court has said about certiorari petitions from at-large accused.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-criticism argument: CA's conduct as a textbook case of how flight from justice undermines the rule of law

stances.claim: The GMA case should be decided via oral argument rather than an ex parte TRO, because an ex parte TRO would practically decide the entire case without any hearing — contrary to the transparent and fair process the paramount constitutional question deserves.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-fairness recommendation: oral argument as the appropriate mechanism for a constitutionally significant, politically charged case

notable_anecdotes: The in flagrante/hot pursuit paradox: the Parañaque police used these doctrines to promptly arrest RJ Bautista but inexplicably did not also arrest Ramona at the same time — if the arrest rationale was valid for RJ, it was equally valid for the co-conspirator Ramona, making her flight entirely preventable.

Lacson's 14-month flight (January 4, 2010 – March 26, 2011) ending only after the CA dismissed his charges while he was still at large — the CA's dismissal 'encouraged lawlessness' but also set the legal precedent that certiorari can be filed while the accused is at large, a legally correct but morally troubling outcome.

The DOJ Circular 41 irony (also noted in A517): the very instrument De Lima used to restrict GMA's travel was issued during GMA's own administration — reducing the elaborate legal argument about constitutional rights to the self-defeating image of a former president being restrained by her own administrative order.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses Senator Bong Revilla Jr.'s statement that 'flight is an admission of guilt' -- triggered by his half-sister Ramona's flight to Turkey the day after Ramgen's murder -- to survey the legal doctrine and three parallel cases of flight by criminal suspects. The SC doctrine (People v. Ayupan, 2002) holds that 'unexplained flight' may be taken as evidence of guilt -- but flight is damning only when unexplained and unrebutted. He applies this to three cases: Ramona Bautista (co-conspirator allowed to fly despite the same in flagrante/hot pursuit rationale used to arrest brother RJ -- an inexplicable police inconsistency now requiring passport cancellation, Interpol red notice, and potential extradition from Turkey); Sen. Lacson (fled January 4, 2010; hid for 14 months until the CA dismissed his Dacer-Corbito double murder charges February 3, 2011 while he was still at large -- which CJ says 'encouraged lawlessness,' though the CA correctly noted the SC allows certiorari from at-large accused; new indictment remains possible since no arraignment occurred); and GMA Arroyo (watch-list order under DOJ Circular 41 issued during her own administration; her constitutional right-to-travel argument complicated by Marcos v. Manglapus which balanced that right against national security even without a specific law). CJ recommends oral argument rather than an ex parte TRO for GMA's petition, applying Holmes's principle that 'general propositions do not decide specific cases.'
